I told myself that if I could not find another job in journalism within a little over a year, I would change careers completely.
Fortunately, I eventually found my way back, working again as both a reporter and news presenter.

items.title: Bangladesh weighs tougher cyber law as AI-generated abuse targets women

s: State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history in the country
Bangladesh is revising its cyber law to tackle AI-generated images, and the draft has triggered a furious debate over how much the state should police speech online.
The ICT Division published the draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act for public comment in mid-September.
It is now with a five-member cabinet committee led by Posts, Telecommunications and ICT Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam.
In a discussion reported on October 19, media figures, legal analysts, and civil society representatives called for the most contested clauses to be removed.
The push follows a campaign season crowded with synthetic media.
Global Voices previously reported on a study that identified 72 AI-manipulated items that gained traction between December 2025 and the February 12, 2026 election.
Synthetic images of political figures were the most common tactic, alongside doctored news-channel graphics.
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which went on to win, was the most frequent target, with 47 cases.
State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history.
Section 57 of the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Act of 2006 punished online content seen as defamatory, hurtful to religious sentiment, or damaging to the state’s image.
A 2013 amendment toughened it, with sentences of up to 14 years.
Journalists and ordinary social media users were among those charged under it.
After years of protest, the government promised to scrap Section 57.
Yet when the Digital Security Act (DSA) was signed into law in October 2018, the same offenses reappeared in sections 25, 28, 29 and 31.
By 2023, the law minister had told parliament that 7,001 cases had been filed under it.
The writer Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody in 2021 after ten months in jail under the DSA, which led to protests at home and abroad.
The Awami League government replaced the DSA with the Cyber Security Act in 2023, but Amnesty International said it repackaged almost all of the DSA’s repressive features.
After the July 2024 uprising, the interim government scrapped nine sections through a new Cyber Security Ordinance in 2025.
Rights groups say hundreds of cases from earlier years are still pending.
Women in politics faced a particular kind of attack.

A Daily Star analysis of AI content before the vote found that pro-Awami League pages targeted female leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) with fabricated images that hinted at moral and sexual impropriety.
After the election, a Prothom Alo fact-check found AI-generated images and invented statements aimed at nominees for reserved women's seats.
Tanvir Mahatab Abir of Rumor Scanner told the paper that visible women, especially in politics, are frequent targets of disinformation.
Not all of it is political.

Data from the Daily Star shows that Facebook pages used deepfake videos of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his family, including his daughter Zaima Rahman, to promote fake “Family Card” offers in exchange for likes and follows.
Among 52 posts analyzed, 13 featured Zaima.
One page administrator told the fact-checking outlet Dismislab that the aim was to gain followers quickly and sell the pages.
In such cases, for many creators of synthetic content, monetization metrics on social platforms often serve as a primary driver alongside political motives.
For ordinary women, the damage can last much longer.
Farzana Sithi, a student activist known for her role in the historic student-led uprising in 2024, was targeted by a fake Facebook profile that Dismislab investigated in March 2025.
Of 166 videos and reels posted between December 13, 2024, and March 17, 2025, 133 were AI-generated deepfakes.
They placed her face on videos of two Indian content creators.
The five most-viewed clips drew more than 4.1 million views, and the account was monetized through Facebook's Stars feature.

items.title: Support Global Voices’ Spotlight: Justice as infrastructure

s: Donate to our Justice as infrastructure Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
All images via Canva or fair use.
Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube.
International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0.
St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience.
But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function.

Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.
Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning.

Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better.
It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential.
Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced.
When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business.
When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital.
When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes.
When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

items.title: Warning Signals: Venezuela and the Risk of AI-Powered Chinese Digital Authoritarianism

s: Venezuela could become an early adopter of China’s AI-powered mass surveillance systems.
Former president of Venezuela Nicolás Maduro with current Interim President Delcy Rodríguez and Chinese ambassador in Venezuela Lan Hu.
Photo by Probox.
Used with permission.

Venezuela may be one step away from becoming one of the first countries outside the People’s Republic of China to adopt the new generation of Chinese artificial intelligence systems for mass surveillance and political control, according to a report from the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI).

The report reveals that in July 2025, the Venezuelan government signed a memorandum of understanding with iFlytek, a Chinese company that has been on the U.S. trade sanctions list since 2019 for its role in the repression of Muslim minorities in Xinjiang.
The agreement to jointly develop Artificial intelligence in Venezuela was negotiated by Delcy Rodríguez, then vice president and now Venezuela’s interim president.

The report was written by Fergus Ryan, Bethany Allen, and Nathan Attrill of ASPI’s Cybersecurity, Technology, and Security Program, along with external contributors Mariví Marín (executive director of ProBox ), Shannon van Sant, and analyst Alex Colville.
The report was published in September 2026 by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, with funding from the Human Rights Foundation.

The report, titled “Warning Signals: Venezuela and the Risk of Chinese AI-Enabled Digital Authoritarianism”, documents that Venezuela doesn’t need to build a surveillance system from scratch — it already has one, built largely on Chinese technology through importing cameras, networks, identity systems and command centres from Chinese firms in the past two decades.

While the resulting architecture is fragmented, unevenly deployed and technically constrained, ASPI's researchers identified six interconnected technological layers in the imported surveillance system: telecommunications, digital identity, central databases, video surveillance, internet control, and now, analytics and artificial intelligence.
All of them were built or enhanced with support from companies such as Huawei, ZTE, CEIEC, Hikvision, and Dahua.
At the core of this system’s identity layer is the Carnet de la Patria (Homeland Card), a digital ID linked to social benefits.
The report states it had 21.8 million registered users as of January 2023—roughly three-quarters of Venezuela’s population—and served as many as 14.2 million people each month.
A layer of central databases could cross-reference identity information, biometric data, and social welfare data.

The report also describes a network of video surveillance and command centres (such as the VEN911 and SIMA systems) capable of monitoring public spaces and coordinating responses in real time, and a telecommunications infrastructure that, by channelling a large portion of the country’s data traffic, functions as an additional checkpoint.

While the above technologies were imported through separate contracts, they reinforce one another and form a partially connected surveillance system, enabl ing government agencies to identify, monitor, and take action regarding citizens’ behaviour.

According to the repo rt, iFlytek's AI technology will further integrate the pre-existing layers of surveillance infrastructure into a more comprehensive system, maki ng it faster, more scalable, and harder to evade.

Facial recognition, voice identification, and automated database cross-referencing tools could be used to identify, locate, and profile individuals without any visible human action, such as attending a protest.
iFlytek is one of the world’s leading providers of voice recognition and content moderation technology.

The same report explains that the company promotes a product capable of detecting “more than 100 types” of politically sensitive content in voice messages, and that its technology is integrated into China’s judicial and censorship system.

iFlytek itself already sells a voiceprint identification service that compares recordings against a database to identify a person among thousands; this is precisely the same technology the company has provided to public security authorities in Xinjiang, according to ASPI's report.

items.title: Fish scarcity, tar balls, and stranded dolphins: The hidden costs of offshore platforms in Cameroon waters

s: Oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities
Offshore platform from Garand-Batanga Beach, Kribi South region of Cameroon.
Photo by Leocadia Bongben.
Used with permission.
This story by Leocadia Bongben was produced with the support of Internews’ Earth Journalism Network.
Dede Sluk, 35, a father of three, sits pensively in front of his plank house, fishing nets hanging at the corner, wondering how to fish for his family and prepare his children for school.
Sluk lives in the village of Grand-Batanga 2 in Kribi, in southern Cameroon.
Like many fishermen there, Sluk is annoyed by the lack of access to fish beyond the offshore platforms. He states,
We don’t have access to areas with high fish stock; the Battaillon D’intervention Rapid (BIR), a special army unit guarding the petroleum platform, prohibits passage.
According to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative’s (EITI) 2023 report, oil and gas contributed FCFA 774.51 billion (USD 1.3 million) to Cameroon’s budget.
However, these oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities.

Offshore oil and gas platforms are massive marine structures used to explore, drill, extract, and process petroleum and natural gas from rocky layers beneath the ocean floor; some require the laying of pipes.
The yellow flames and smoke from the Ebome Marine Terminal, a petroleum rig operated by Perenco and SNH west of Grand Batanga, are visible 6.5 kilometers (4.04 miles) from the Kribi coastline.
Two other platforms are the Sanaga 2 offshore facility around Kribi, connected via undersea pipelines from onshore in Bipaga.
West of the Kribi Port is the Kome-Kribi 1 Terminal (FSO), built in 2003, operated by Cameroon Oil Transport Company — the Chad-Cameroon pipeline.
Meanwhile, the Hilli Episeyo, operated by Golar LNG, Perenco, and the National Hydrocarbons Corporation (SNH), departed in July 2026, after eight years.

Among the platforms of concern are those operated by Perenco, a Franco-British company and a prominent player in the oil and gas sector, tagged as an opaque multinational by Friends of the Earth for oil spills, wastewater discharges, gas flaring, and old pipelines crossing rivers.
An Info Congo investigation indicted Perenco for flaring and environmental hazards, endangering the coastal ecosystem and the health of local communities.

Tar balls found in a marine protected area, dolphin and whale strandings, and fish scarcity are hidden costs of offshore oil and gas exploitation, which seems to stall Cameroon’s progress towards the 30×30 marine target under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Laure Ndingue, 50, a mother of five who worked as a fish roaster along Grand Batanga beach for over 10 years, knows that, opposite her charcoal braise, an oil and gas platform sits in the ocean.
She recalls,
Growing up, six barfish were sold for FCFA 500 (USD 0.85); the price jumped to FCFA 1,000 (USD 1.70) and now is FCFA 5000 (USD 8.54) per kilogram.
Even frozen fish is now expensive.
Before, we were not suffering; fish stocks have declined.
Petroleum exploitation is done when the platform is planted on a rock, and most times, the rocks are marine ecosystems that breed fish.

Now, the rocks are occupied by offshore installations, contributing to reduced fish stocks, explains Divine Francois Xavier Mbunje, a fisherman, geologist, and president of the 150-fishermen union at the Grand Batanga beach.
He suggests the government can demarcate platforms and areas of high fish concentration.
About a kilometer or two from the beach, there is no fish, and three kilometers deep, we can have around forty kilograms of fish.

Sluk proposes that oil and gas platforms should help the local population with activities like fish farming, loans to make up for the fish scarcity, recommending that the government provide a loan scheme and subsidize the purchase of motorized equipment, as this will help the fishers go further into the ocean.

items.title: Volunteers from Poland remember how Poles opened their homes to Ukrainian refugees in 2022

s: Now, Russian disinformation fuels the memory of violent historic conflicts, and Polish empathy is burning out

Folkowisko during the “Borderland Memory” project, bringing Ukrainian and Polish youth together to preserve shared historical heritage, restore historic cemeteries, and strengthen cross-cultural friendship.
Photo: Folkowisko.
Used with permission.
Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there.
Nobody was helping them.”
People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius.
On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own.
Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene.
“We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains.
“We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well.
Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”
What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border.
Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops.
The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.
But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present.
Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation.
“Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland.
“Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish.
People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula.
This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”
The history separating the two societies is particularly painful.
During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region.
Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians.
The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.
After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate.

In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.
Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation.
He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains.
“It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred.
Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

items.title: Vote young yet govern much later: West African youth’s struggle for power

s: In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Youth mobilized in Africa.
Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel
In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18.
In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25.
However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office.
Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.
Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them.
They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves.
The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?
Across the region, the voting age is 18.
However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely.
In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40.
In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower.
In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.
The situation in Togo requires closer inspection.
On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic.
Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50.
Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited.
Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections.
Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.
However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone.
In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.

More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30.
This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.
In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent.
Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.
According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments.
However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story.
In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025.
The law rarely protects younger generations.
Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right.
In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation.
Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal.
Protests were the only exception.
In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets.
According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights ( FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.

items.title: Queer mediums of the cult of María Lionza are redefining the gender binary in Venezuela’s sacred mountain

s: Gender diversity, resistance and ritual cross-dressing in Venezuela's sacred cult
Portrait of Wander Rodríguez, part of the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers, and the LGBTIQ+ community.
Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.
In Venezuela, Spiritism as a religion is part of the collective imagination, of our identity; popular beliefs and ritual practices that take us back to our ancestors in colonial times.

Over the years, Spiritism has evolved into a vibrant, contemporary national cult centered on the figure of María Lionza as the principal protector of waters and the charms of nature, a figure who challenges the notions of the patriarchal state and opposes monotheistic religions.

This religious system has been studied in depth by anthropologists in our country ( Daisy Barreto, Angelina Pollak-Eltz, Michelle Asencio, Francisco Ferrándiz, Cesar Escalona, among others), which I had read about and found interesting at the time, but which I later witnessed for the first time in its most important sites, such as Quibayo and Sorte, in the state of Yaracuy, Venezuela.
Altar to María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

These sites are part of the Cerro María Lionza Natural Monument, popularly known as the Montaña de Sorte, and they represent the most prominent expressions of this cult nationwide, so they are visited year-round by practitioners or “caravans” (as these groups are commonly called),
But few days are as important as October 11 and 12, when thousands of people flock there to celebrate the Day of Indigenous Resistance in Venezuela.

These dates offer an opportunity for ethnographic and cultural observation, specifically how oral histories and our ethnic origins are reclaimed; including those of Indigenous peoples, some of them warriors who fought against Spanish colonization, and African populations — enslaved people and maroons [AN: this will need context] — as we can understand through the figure of the Three Powers: Queen María Lionza as the central figure of the cult, the leader, accompanied by El Indio Guaicaipuro and El Negro Felipe.
Altar to Queen María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

For this celebration families gather among the trees and along the banks of the Yaracuy River, which runs through the entire mountain, setting up lavish altars to the various deities of Venezuelan spiritualism, which embody the sacred rituals characteristic of the Marialioncero cult.

The figure of María Lionza is profound, and I believe it is risky to oversimplify her, as she is regarded as a Queen, a Goddess, a mother, and a guardian, yet there are also aspects linked to her sensuality, as evidenced by the iconographic representations of her that have emerged -naked or clothed, for example-.

In this regard, I draw upon the writings of Francisco Ferrándiz and César Escalona from the perspective of Venezuelan anthropology, combining them with my own observations and field interviews, to address issues related to gender and sexual diversity that are essential to the fascinating debate within the cult on its various courts — such as the Black Court, the Viking Court, the Malandra Court, the Chamarrera Court, and the Medical Court, among others — and entities.
Detail of flowers and bottles of the Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

The Sorte Mountain is a setting where gender stereotypes are called into question, and I believe they undermine androcentric perspectives and rigid notions of masculinity and femininity found within Christianity, since the entities pose a challenge due to their wide spectrum in terms of strength, height, voice, attire, and other details of the mediums who embody them, as well as the particular characteristics of each spirit.
Strenght between banks and Viking Court entity.
Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

items.title: Between two shores: The ‘Monhés,’ nationality, and a sense of belonging in Mozambique

s: Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname
Indians in Mozambique celebrating the Hindu festival of Navratri.
Image by Kash_if via Flickr. CC BY 2.0.
In Mozambique, the word monhé has a much deeper history than its everyday use might suggest.
Depending on who says it and the context, it can simply be a reference to the population of Indian origin, an identity marker, or a prejudiced remark.
But behind the word there is a history of migration, trade, colonialism, independence, displacement, and, above all, belonging.
The question of who is Mozambican gets particularly interesting when we look at the communities of Indian origin, who have lived in the country for several generations.
Are they Mozambicans? Indians? Foreigners?
Or, in some cases, stateless persons?
The answer cannot be found in appearance, surname, religion, or family origin alone.
It is found in the country’s history and, particularly, in its nationality law.

The presence of people originating from the Indian subcontinent in the lands we now call Mozambique predates the country’s independence and, in many instances, predates the demarcation of the current political borders.
The Indian Ocean’s trade networks connected the East African coast to South Asia long before 1975, the year Mozambique gained its independence.
Over time, merchants, families, and whole communities settled in different parts of the country.
During the Portuguese colonial period, this took place within a political structure that gave people nationalities and legal statuses according to the rules of the empire.
As such, “being of Indian origin” never meant automatically “being an Indian citizen.
A person can have Indian ancestry and at the same time hold Portuguese, Indian, Pakistani, or any other nationality, which could leave people in a complex bureaucratic situation.
This distinction became especially important when the empire came to an end.
Mozambique’s independence, made official on June 25th, 1975, did not just mean a transfer of political power.
It also implied the need to define who would legally receive the new state, which was known as the New State.
The Nationality Law of 1975 was key to answering that question.

Among its provisions were rules that recognized as Mozambicans certain people born in the territory and resident in Mozambique at the time of independence, as well as other criteria related to birth, family links, and residence.
The legislation would thus transform a heterogeneous imperial population into a national political community.

For many families of Indian origin who lived in Mozambique for decades or generations, this transformation would mean a fundamental change: no longer being legally associated with a colonial power or a foreign nationality and becoming part of the new Mozambican nation.
But the experience of this transition was not the same for everybody.
Decolonization created situations where identity, origin, and nationality did not match.
Imagine a family history across three generations: the grandparents born in India, the parents born in Mozambique during the colonial period, and the children born after independence.
Which nationality should each generation have?

The answer may depend on specific legal circumstances: place of birth, the parents’ nationality, residence in Mozambique at its independence, existing documentation, and any decisions to opt for or relinquish nationality.
Here, the issue of statelessness arises.
A stateless person is somebody who is not considered a national by any state’s legislation.
It is not an ambiguous cultural identity or feeling divided between two countries, but a legal status.

After decolonization, some people in former colonial territories, such as Angola and Mozambique, faced this problem: some were no longer recognized as nationals by the former colonial power without any other nationalities automatically being granted.
This does not mean, though, that the whole Indian community in Mozambique became stateless.
This generalization would be historically and legally incorrect.

items.title: Big Tech and authoritarian states: Belarus

s: A Global Voices video podcast on the state of digital repression in Belarus
There are more autocracies in the world in 2026 than there are democracies.
Some researchers identify digital authoritarianism as the use of digital technology by regimes to surveil, repress, and manipulate domestic and foreign populations.
Others argue that the same practices are also carried out by hybrid and democratic regimes.
However, they can not execute them without major tech companies becoming complicit, with or without their knowledge.
Typically, when speaking about digital authoritarianism, academics and media talk about China and Russia (and occasionally Iran and Syria).
However, countries such as Belarus (or Eritrea, Nicaragua, Afghanistan, Myanmar) that consistently rank as more authoritarian than China are rarely discussed.
Global Voices invited an expert on Belarusian internet, digital rights and media, Mikhail Doroshevich, on the GV video podcast “Big Tech and Authoritarian States.

We discussed why Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenka’s regime is not blocking Western social media platforms, how the internet and self-censorship are weaponized, and how platforms help the regime to spread its propaganda.
You can view and listen to the podcast in Russian on our YouTube Channel and read the translated transcript below:
Daria Dergacheva (DD): Hello, dear viewers.
My name is Daria Dergacheva, and welcome to another Global Voices video podcast.
Today we are discussing Big Tech and authoritarian states.
Our guest is Mikhail Doroshevich, who works on digital issues in Belarus.
We will speak in Russian, but an English translation and subtitles will be available.
Please leave your questions in the comments and like the video.
Mikhail, welcome.
Please tell us a little about yourself.
This is the second Global Voices video podcast I have hosted, and today we want to focus on Belarus.
Mikhail Doroshevich (MD): I can describe myself very briefly, in one sentence: I am a researcher who has been studying the Belarusian internet for more than 30 years.
A well-known political scientist once introduced me in a publication as a “veteran of the Belarusian internet.
Since then, I have jokingly used that description myself.
But let us talk about something more interesting.
DD: Being a veteran of the Belarusian internet is interesting in itself!
I would also like to talk about its history and what is happening now.
I recently saw an article from Carnegie suggesting that the internet in Belarus remains considerably more open than in Russia.
I find this paradox fascinating.
How does the Belarusian regime deal with Western, Chinese, and Russian platforms?
MD: That is quite a complicated technical question.
In infrastructural terms, the Belarusian internet has always been more restricted than the Russian internet.
By infrastructure, I mean connectivity and connections to the global internet.
Since the 1990s, Russian internet providers and mobile telecommunications companies have had their own international connections.
Belarus, by contrast, has always had a vulnerable infrastructure.
International connections were controlled by state-owned companies, including the national operator.
Private providers and mobile operators never had their own independent international connections.
Yet today Russia restricts access to many social media services, from LinkedIn onwards, while Belarus does not impose comparable restrictions on those platforms.
So Belarus historically had greater technical constraints, and shutdowns regularly accompanied political campaigns.
Blocking websites and resources designated as extremist or terrorist is still widespread and ongoing.
But Belarus has not followed the path Russia has taken in recent years.
Their technological approaches have diverged.
DD: Do you think the platforms comply with [blocking or takedown] requests from the Belarusian state?
Why is this happening?

items.title: In Brazil’s elections, big techs’ transparency and cooperation policies translate as governance washing, according to this expert

s: Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University NetLab has been following closely how this election unfolds on social media
Amid a series of corruption scandals, the 2026 general election in Brazil is also flooded with headlines about social media companies’ role in the campaign.

Users supporting the candidacy of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent center-left candidate running for re-election, have been reporting a sudden drop in their Instagram Stories views when posting about politics.

They say that Meta AI refused to generate images featuring Lula’s name and party number, while delivering the same request for Flávio Bolsonaro, his far-right opponent and the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro.
On October 16, Meta admitted technical problems on its platforms which affected how pro-Lula content was delivered to users.

As reported by the Associated Press, despite acknowledging “global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures, and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression,” the company that owns Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook denied any political bias.

Lula filed a complaint against Meta accusing the company of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election, with a judge from the country’s top electoral court ruling that Meta must adopt measures to ensure equal treatment.
With an estimated population of 214 million, Brazil is an important market for social media platforms.
It ranks as the second country by number of WhatsApp users and saw the internet become a key component of Jair Bolsonaro’s ascent around 10 years ago.

To understand the current election scenario, Global Voices spoke to Nicole Sanchotene, project coordinator at NetLab, a research laboratory at Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University (UFRJ) that has been publishing reports on the impact of big tech on the electoral campaign.
The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Global Voices: What have you identified in NetLab’s recent reports about the elections?
Nicole Sanchotene: É muito difícil avaliar o impacto e os possíveis efeitos para a disputa eleitoral e para a percepção das pessoas.

O problema central que a gente tem apontado é sobre transparência, uma certa normalização de possíveis ilícitos eleitorais, pontos que são consenso na resolução do TSE (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral) e não estamos vendo cumprimento pleno das plataformas.
O Kwai, que é uma plataforma com ampla adesão no Brasil, tem mais de 60 milhões de usuários, é bastante usado pelas classes C e D, fez uma parceria com o TSE e não está adequado.
Não atende a requisitos básicos, a biblioteca de anúncios político-eleitorais tem falhas no tipo de dado que entrega.
A gente tem chamado essas práticas de transparência de fachada.
Cada uma das plataformas tem um problema específico.
Seja por dados incompletos, seja pela veiculação ou recomendação de conteúdo que não deveria ser recomendado.

O que a gente vê é que elas não estão respeitando plenamente o que é exigido pelas normas brasileiras para garantir um mínimo de condições de igualdade para os candidatos, condições que permitam um ambiente de informação, de propaganda, seguro para os usuários e para a disputa eleitoral.
Nicole Sanchotene: It’s hard to evaluate the impact and possible effects on the running and on people’s perception.

The central issue that we’ve been pointing to is transparency, a certain normalization of possible illicit electoral practices, issues that were agreed upon in the TSE [Superior Electoral Court, Brazil's top electoral court] resolution, and we are not seeing the platforms comply fully.

Kwai, a platform with widespread adoption in Brazil, with over 60 million users and largely used by “ C and D classes ” [lower income groups and the basis of the socio-economic pyramid], partnered with the electoral court, and it’s not suitable yet.
It doesn't meet basic requirements; their library for political-electoral ads has flaws in the data delivered.
We have been calling this a ‘façade of transparency.’

items.title: US President Donald Trump appears to wear makeup after apparent rash breaks out on neck, reports say

s: On Tuesday, a rash that reporters had observed on US President Donald Trump's neck in photos from a Medal of Honor ceremony at the White House one day earlier appeared to have been covered up.
One media source indicated the substance used was cosmetic makeup, although Trump's physician, Dr. Sean Barbabella, told the source the rash had been covered up by a "very common cream."
President Trump has worn makeup in public before.
He once wore makeup to obscure bruises on his hands, which White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, stated were inflicted from "shaking hands all day every day.
Trump himself has attributed the bruises to his use of aspirin, of which he says he takes excessive amounts.
Trump said, "They say aspirin is good for thinning out the blood, and I don’t want thick blood pouring through my heart.
I want nice, thin blood pouring through my heart.
Does that make sense?"

items.title: Monta publishes its 2025 EV charger ranking, including hardware performance

s: The Danish firm Monta published a performance ranking of electric vehicle (EV) chargers on Wednesday.
The firm analysed 260,000 EV chargers connected to its platform, which were located in Europe.
In the publication, the firm showed the chargers ranked by their "performance score".
The firm calculated this score metric from two parameters — the charger uptime, and the percent of charge sessions that went successful without hardware or software or user interruptions.
The AC — slower chargers — and DC — fast chargers — ranking was provided in two separate tables.
AC chargers performance was topped by a Mennekes EV charger, with performance score 94.65.
Among DC chargers, five charger models by Alpitronic took the top spots, with performance score reaching 96.54.

The Driven, an Australian news site, noted that '9 out of 10' of the top performing DC chargers from Monta's report were available for sale, and were in use — by Ampol AmpCharge and BP Pulse — in Australia.
The firm noted the published results provided motivation for EV chargers to adopt these benchmarks in marketing, and further develop their products to increase performance and uptime.

A volunteer Wikinews reporter reached out to Monta, and Monta has clarified that they also have some EV chargers on their platform in Asia, Oceania, and North America, however excluded them from the ranking due to small quantities.
Monta also noted they were planning to release quarterly EV charger updates in 2026, and yearly EV charger ranking reports with awards.
The Monta's EV charger ranking program was launched in June last year.
Monta won the best EV app/software at the E-Mobility Awards 2023.

items.title: Moreton Bay illegally evicted homeless campers, Queensland Supreme Court rules

s: This past Friday, Justice Paul Smith of the Supreme Court of Queensland ruled that the City of Moreton Bay Council, immediately north of Brisbane, Australia, acted unlawfully when it removed several homeless people camping in public parks last year.

The court concluded the Council breached the law by providing insufficient time for the homeless people to find alternative accommodation and by disposing of their personal belongings without consent.

In the judgement, Justice Smith said the Council made "errors of law" finding that the Council's seizure and disposal of the property of eight homeless people at Eddie Hyland Park — including their tents and other personal belongings — without consent in April and May last year violated human rights.
Although the eviction involved eight campers at the park, the legal case was brought by eleven applicants who said they were affected by the Council's enforcement actions.
The judgement noted that the Council would still be allowed to remove campers from public parks provided this was done "lawfully".
On Friday, the Council published a statement noting that eight homeless people had taken the Council to court and linking to the Supreme Court judgement.
In that statement Council stated it would continue enforcing its ban on camping on public land.
Responsibility for providing shelter to homeless people rested with the Queensland state government according to the Council.
The court scheduled the next hearing in three weeks to determine relief and costs.
Basic Rights Queensland and the Queensland Human Rights Commission supported the campers in the legal proceedings.
The Council's actions followed its decision earlier in February last year to ban camping on public land, which made camping illegal on public land within the Council from March 12, 2025.

items.title: Australia grants refuge to five Iranian women's national soccer team players

s: Early Tuesday morning, Australia government officials issued humanitarian visas to five members of Iran's national women's football team.

The players refused to sing the Iranian anthem while at the Women's Asian Cup last week. if the visas had not been granted, the five players potentially faced serious punishment on their return to Iran, as Iranian media has labeled them "traitors".
Tony Burke, Minister for Home Affairs of Australia, sent a message on X on Tuesday stating that the five players were "welcome to stay in Australia, to be safe and have a home here".
The players are Zahra Ghanbari (captain), Fatemeh Pasandideh, Zahra Sarbali, Atefeh Ramezanizadeh, and Mona Hamoudi.
Tuesday afternoon, however, the rest of the Iranian national women's soccer team travelled to Gold Coast airport by bus.
As of Tuesday morning, authorities said these remaining Iranian women's soccer team members had not requested asylum, though were welcomed to do so.
Protesters surrounded the bus and some were lying on the ground to stop the bus, and had to be moved by police.

Due to reported threats from Iranian media and officials, in Australia, local police worked with the authorities and provided a safe place for the players to stay, as well as increased presence when the players were traveling.

items.title: Former Major League Baseball pitcher Julio Teherán retires

s: Julio Teherán, a two-time Major League Baseball All-Star, announced his retirement from baseball on Monday, at the age of 35.
The decision came two days after he was scratched from a scheduled start for Team Colombia in the 2026 World Baseball Classic (WBC) due to a shoulder injury.
Teherán had helped Team Colombia secure a 3-1 victory over Team Panama in the WBC before announcing his retirement.
Teherán had a thirteen-year MLB career, during which he primarily played for the Atlanta Braves, but also played for the Los Angeles Angels, Detroit Tigers, Milwaukee Brewers, and New York Mets.
He made his MLB debut with the Braves in 2011 at the age of 20 and spent his first nine seasons with the team, earning All-Star selections in 2014 and 2016.
Over his MLB career, Teherán compiled a 81-82 record, with a 3.85 ERA, 1.223 WHIP, and 1,260 strikeouts in 1,470.2 innings.
He had spent the 2022 and 2025 seasons playing in the Mexican Baseball League.

items.title: PM of Australia sends E-7A Wedgetail and air-to-air missiles to UAE

s: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that, in response to United Arab Emirates call for help, Australia would deploy E-7A Wedgetail, a long-range reconnaissance plane, to help Gulf Arab states defend against attacks from Iran.
The Australian Defence Force said the plane is able to survey four million square kilometers with a powerful radar.
Government officials said the plane would be manned by around 85 Australian defence force (ADF) personnel.
Additionally, Australia would supply middle range air to air missiles, at the request of United Arab Emirates, that could down enemy's drones.
Foreign affairs correspondent at ABC News, Stephen Dziedzic, published a piece on Wednesday noting that from a legal perspective, Australia is at war.
He stated that not being an attacker, and not entering Iran, did not preclude Australia from joining a war.

The correspondent referenced article 51 from United Nations charter about "collective self-defence", which could involve, for example, providing support or intelligence to one of the participants of a war.
The correspondent raised concern that move could make Australia a potential target for attacks from, for example, Iran.

items.title: NSW government proposes rezoning to create residences midway between Sydney and Parramatta

s: The government of New South Wales (NSW), Australia announced plans to rezone the 113-hectare Burwood North precinct this Tuesday.
The plan included building 18,300 new homes in the area, and building a new metro station.
This would position the area as a residential hub between Sydney CBD and Parramatta, shortening commute times down to ten minutes, the proposal said.

With allowance for up to 42 storey residential buildings, the government proposal involved a requirement that at least 5% of the new homes were "affordable housing", offered at a lower rental price to lower income households.
Burwood North Station, scheduled to open in 2032, would provide easier access to retail outlets and businesses located near Parramatta Road, and reduce load on existing train and bus networks.
The proposal text noted it would create 3,900 new jobs to implement the changes.
The proposal was a part of Parramatta Road Corridor Urban Transformation Strategy.
The NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure was listed as a contact for inquiries and feedback.

items.title: US president Donald Trump demands the unconditional surrender of Iran

s: Last Friday, United States President Donald Trump demanded the "unconditional surrender" of Iran via his Truth Social platform.
The declaration came as the war in Iran had gone on for a week.
Trump has also demanded more "acceptable" leadership in the country.
Trump wrote that once "acceptable" leadership was selected in Iran, the US and its allies would make Iran "economically bigger, better, and stronger than ever before."
On Saturday, in an address to the nation, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Trump's demand is a "dream they should send to their grave."
A week ago, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, and killed various government officials, including the supreme leader of Iran, Ali Khamenei, in strikes.
In retaliation for the attacks, Iran has bombed Middle Eastern countries including Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, according to SBS News.
In the Saturday address, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian apologized for attacks on regional countries, Jakarta Globe reported.
The Globe also reported that 1,230 people were killed in Iran and that six US troops were killed.
Leavitt has stated that the war would likely last four to six weeks.

items.title: Australian Minister for Energy lowers fuel standards for 60 days amid rising oil prices, panic buying

s: Chris Bowen, Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, allowed the usage of dirtier fuel with elevated sulfur content for 60 days, he announced on Thursday.
As a part of the change, the oil refineries were required to prioritise supply to farmers in rural areas.
This decision followed issues with oil exports caused by the ongoing Middle East conflict, as fuel prices rose rapidly to over A$2/L.
The lower quality oil was previously exported to countries with lower fuel standards.
With the new temporarily changes in place, it would now be allowed to be used in Australia.
One of the two oil refineries, Ampol, noted rural areas supply would be prioritised.
Additionally, Bowen announced Australia would release 100 million liters from its reserve oil supply per month, in response to a request from the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The issue appeared related to the growing demand while supply was essentially unchanged.
As people stockpiled fuel, and the demand has doubled, there were concerns over panic buying by Australians.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese commented on longer term impacts of the situation on economics in Australia, talking with ABC Television on Thursday.

President of the National Farmer Federation commented noting the government regulation was direly needed in this situation as farmers and fishers were struggling to access fuel, especially in remote areas.

He also noted that government should prepare strategies in case the situation 'deteriorates', mentioning access to diesel was a pre-requisite for the farmers running the agricultural areas, collecting crops, transporting crops, and providing food to the country.
In reserve, Australia had 36 days worth of petrol, 32 days worth of diesel, and 29 days worth of jet fuel, respectively.
These fell short of the 90 days requirement under obligations for the IEA, of which Australia is a member.
Opposition was calling on the government to ensure fuel security, ABC News reported.

items.title: Caloundra win round 3 game in Australian soccer's Football Queensland Premier League 2 competition

s: Caloundra have won their round 3 Football Queensland Premier League 2 game against Pine Hills 5 goals to 2 at Meridan Plains, Queensland, Australia on Sunday.
"Two [wins] from three [games]" said Caloundra captain Kaine Frew.
"I think we'll probably be in the top four now.
Not a bad start.
It's still very early days.
Yeah, you can't get too ahead of yourselves.
I think you've just got to take it week by week for the moment."
Riley Campbell opened the scoring for Caloundra in the second minute.
Aaron Doherty levelled the score two minutes later.
Alex Witte took Pine Hills ahead in the eleventh minute.
Darryl Barton brought the scores level again in the thirteenth minute.
Barton scored his second goal to retake the lead do Caloundra in the twenty seventh minute.
Caloundra lead three goals to two at the break.
Jake Debbage added Caloundra's fourth in the fifty first minute before Mackenar Bradfield took the score line to five goals to three in the ninetieth minute.
"It was a pretty even game, first half," said Pine Hills assistant coach Daniel Cunha.
"[We] conceded three goals.
Lazy goals, in our opinion.
But we managed to bounce back with two goals.
Managed to stay in the game, but yeah, second half with early, conceded early goals, so that was it for us."
Caloundra host Mitchellton on Saturday, while Pine Hills travel to Samford.

items.title: "One Battle After Another" wins 6 Oscars including Best Picture

s: One Battle After Another was the big winner at the 98th Academy Awards ceremony, held on Sunday, March 15 at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, California.
The film received six Oscars including Best Picture.
Director Paul Thomas Anderson personally won Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay, in addition to being one of the producers who received the Best Picture award.

The other three Oscars which One Battle After Another received were for Best Editing and Best Casting, the first time the latter award has been presented, and for Sean Penn as Best Supporting Actor, the third Oscar of his career.
Sinners, which had set a record by earning sixteen Oscar nominations, won awards in four categories: Best Actor for Michael B.
Jordan, Best Original Screenplay for Ryan Coogler, Best Original Score for Ludwig Goransson, and Best Cinematography for Autumn Durald Arkapaw.
Arkapaw is the first woman to win an Academy Award for Best Cinematography.
Two other films won multiple Oscars.
Frankenstein won Best Production Design, Best Costume Design, and Best Makeup and Hairstyling.
KPop Demon Hunters won Best Animated Feature and Best Song for Golden.
Best Supporting Actress: Amy Madigan for Weapons
Best International Feature: Sentimental Value, from Norway (directed by Joachim Trier)
Best Visual Effects: Avatar: Fire and Ash
Best Documentary Feature: Mr. Nobody Against Putin
Best Documentary Short: All the Empty Rooms
Best Animated Short: The Girl Who Cried Pearls
Best Live Action Short: The Singers and Two People Exchanging Saliva (tie)
The Oscar ceremony was hosted by Conan O'Brien.

items.title: South Korean military halts small firearms drills after stray bullet strikes young girl on playground

s: On Tuesday, officials for the South Korean Army said at a press conference that they were suspending all scheduled drills involving smaller firearms such as rifles and handguns.

The decision was made in response to an incident earlier in the week on Monday that resulted in a young girl at a children playground in Daegu being injured near the neck by an alleged stray bullet from a military drill at nearby military facility.
Her injuries were not life-threatening and she was released from the hospital.
Her name was not released to the general public.
Investigations into the circumstances leading up the incident were said to be underway.
The incident raised questions regarding the military's practice of conducting shooting drills in close proximity to civilian territory.
A spokesperson for the army confirmed that a firearms drill had indeed been taking place at the same time the girl reported being struck.
The incident came a year after the South Korean Army accidentally bombed a small village near the North Korean border, injuring 30 civilians, while conducting a drill with US forces.

items.title: Musique Libre Femmes plays for Women's History Month at Tompkins Square Library in New York City

s: On Thursday, March 12, 2026, the Tompkins Square Library in New York City hosted a concert by Musique Libre Femmes, in its basement performance space.
This performance featured Cheryl Pyle on flute, Ayumi Ishito on saxophones, and Roberta Piket on piano.
There were approximately fifteen people in attendance.
Wikinews attended the event and took several photos and recordings to transcribe for this news report.
The performance started at 6:00 p.m.
New York Time (2200 UTC), and was introduced by director of adult services Jeffrey Katz.
After explaining that the series was ongoing, and announcing upcoming performance dates as well, he introduced the performers:
((Jeffrey Katz)) So we are celebrating Women's History Month with Musique Libre Femmes.
And this is a group of all women free jazz improvisers who compose, create spontaneous, in-the-moment music.
The group consists of some of the most experienced improvisers of the New York Jazz scene.
And they have recently played at the Lady Got Chops Festival, the Downtown Music Gallery, and many of the New York City Jazz venues.
After which, the performance began and lasted about forty minutes, after which the audience applauded.
After the event, Pyle had the following comments about the series:

((Cheryl Pyle)) I started the group Musique Libre Femmes, Free Music Women, because I saw a film called Fire Music, and they interviewed Carla Bley and Ingrid Sertso, and they didn't talk about any of their music.
And they didn't talk about any other women improvisers, Barbara Donald, you know, anybody.
So I wanted to do some concerts with all women.
((CP)) And today we played with Roberta Piket on piano and Ayumi Ishito on tenor sax and soprano sax and myself, Cheryl Pyle on C-flute, piccolo and alto flute.
And we're here at the Tompkins Square Library in the East Village and we just had a wonderful concert.

items.title: United States announces blockade on the Strait of Hormuz

s: On Sunday, United States President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that the US is imposing a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Trump, the blockade was in effect as of 10:00 a.m.
Eastern Time (1400 UTC).
The blockade was imposed following the collapse of talks held in Islamabad between the United States and Iran.
"Effective immediately, the United States Navy, the finest in the world, will be BLOCKADING any and all ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz," Trump declared.
According to The Guardian, oil prices briefly rose above US$100 a barrel following news of the blockade, before easing back to just over US$99; gas prices also increased.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf posted on X to "Enjoy the current pump figures.
With the so-called 'blockade', soon you'll be nostalgic for $4–$5 gas.
He further stated that Iran would respond in kind to both escalation and diplomacy, warning that it would "fight" if confronted militarily but would "deal with logic" if approached constructively.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed hope that the ceasefire would remain stable, stating that Beijing is willing to cooperate with all parties to "guarantee the uninterrupted flow of energy supplies," and that stability in the Strait of Hormuz is critically important to China.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV visits four nations in Africa

s: Pope Leo XIV arrived by plane in Algeria on Monday, April 13, beginning his apostolic visit to Africa.

A senior Vatican official told the BBC the pope wanted to "turn the world's attention to Africa"; the BBC reported the eleven-day visit would address themes of peace, migration, and interfaith dialogue.
The trip also includes stops in Cameroon, Angola, and Equatorial Guinea.
The visit marked Leo's second major foreign trip as pope since his election in May last year.
The regions of the continent being visited are among the quickest growing in Catholicism in the world.
There were an estimated 288 million Catholics in Africa in 2024, making up more than one-fifth of the world's total.
His first stop in Algeria marked the first papal visit to the country in history.
While there, Leo planned to visit several locations including ancient Christian sites in Annaba and the Great Mosque of Algiers in the capital before departing.

The stop was followed by a visit to Cameroon, where Leo addressed about 120,000 people in Douala, encouraging young people to turn away from violence and corruption and advocating for justice and peace.
He was expected to make a planned visit to a Catholic hospital in the city before traveling to Yaoundé to meet with students from the Catholic University of Central Africa.
On Sunday, April 19, the pope arrived in Angola, where he met with President João Lourenço and other officials.
He later addressed a crowd gathered near the capital, Luanda.
He was also expected to visit the town of Muxima, the country's main Christian pilgrimage site.

After Angola, the pope arrived on Tuesday, April 21, in Equatorial Guinea, where, according to the BBC, Catholics make up more than 70% of the central African nation, for the final leg of the visit, before his scheduled return to the Vatican.

items.title: Wikimedia Foundation closes Wikinews after 21 years

s: The Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation announced on March 30 its decision to close all language editions of the project.

In the announcement, a representative from Wikimedia Foundation cited motivations such as "long-term sustainability, levels of community activity, and the availability of reliable news coverage on other platforms".
The announcement stated that all Wikinews editions—referring to the multiple language sections of Wikinews—would "transition to read-only mode" on May 4.
The announcement did not mention the time zone when the wiki would go in read-only mode; but Wikinews operated under the UTC timezone.

In the announcement message, WMF trustee Victoria Doronina said, "We thank all contributors who have participated in Wikinews over the years and helped build a unique experiment in collaborative journalism within the Wikimedia movement.
We understand that some of them may be disappointed by this decision.
To our regret, the project wasn't able to fulfil its promise, and many of its functions were eclipsed by the notable news coverage in Wikipedias."
According to the WMF, most traffic to Wikinews came in the form of web crawlers and bots, as opposed to humans.
Per the Wikimedia Cloud statistics in the past one year, both, English and Chinese Wikinews received more traffic from humans as compared to crawlers.
The foundation stated in its closure recommendation that it is "difficult to claim that it is disseminating educational content and, even more so, that it is doing so effectively and globally."
On March 31, users from different countries and regions started discussions regarding moving the Wikinews content and community to another website at Wikimedia's Meta-Wiki.

Miraheze and Wikimedia NYC were in discussion of continuing the hosting as Wikinews Pulse, with a restructure to increase multilingual support and try new outputs, according to a note by a Wikimedia volunteer User:Pharos.
However, at the time of publishing this report, they had not provided an estimated time the project would be restarted.
Wikinews was a sister project of other Wikimedia initiatives.
Some of the other sister projects includes Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and Wikimedia Commons.
All of these Wikimedia projects support the dissemination of free knowledge and media.
The future of Wikinews was raised for consideration in June, with a WMF task force recommending the project's closure, followed by a period of public consultation about Wikinews.
After this process, the Board announced in March that the 31 active editions of Wikinews would be placed in read-only mode indefinitely.
Wikinews was launched in November 2004.
It was first proposed by an anonymous contributor in January 2003 and faced a community vote that ended 151 yea and 59 nay, leading to the first demo going live in October 2004.
The English-language Wikinews was formally created December 2 of that year, with German following one day later.
The project's early development followed a series of community discussions and milestones in late 2004 and early 2005.
A non-binding straw poll on content licensing began on October 26, 2004, alongside discussions on the project's scope and policies.
The initial demo site, hosted at demo.wikinews.org, was later moved to the English Wikinews domain on December 2 of that year.

Following the launch of the English and German editions in December 2004, additional language editions were created in early 2005, including Dutch, French, Swedish, Spanish, Bulgarian, Polish, Romanian, and Portuguese.
The project also adopted a logo in February 2005 through a community voting process.
While many Wikinews articles were synthesized from other news sources, the project also posted original reporting.
The purpose of this activity was to add exclusive content which would not be available elsewhere on the web or on television.
These original reports included interviews with people such as Shimon Peres, then-president of Israel; U.S.
Senator Sam Brownback; journalist Gay Talese; and voice actor Billy West.
A 2005 article featuring original reporting, Unrest in Belize, was cited by Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales as Wikinews's first scoop.

items.title: Opposition leader Tarique Rahman returns to Bangladesh after 17 years

s: Tarique Rahman, the acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) returned to Bangladesh on December 25, 2025, landing in Dhaka after 17 years in self-imposed exile in London.
His arrival marks a significant development in the country's political landscape following the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024.
Rahman is the son of Khaleda Zia, the official chairperson of the party and former Prime Minister of Bangladesh.
Upon landing at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, Rahman was greeted by thousands of Bangladesh Nationalist Party supporters amid tight security.

Accompanied by his wife, Zubaida Rahman, and daughter, Zaima Rahman, he addressed a rally, emphasizing national unity, inclusivity across religious lines, and the vision of a democratic and economically strong Bangladesh.
He drew parallels to the country's 1971 war of independence.
Rahman, aged 60, left Bangladesh in 2008 for medical treatment after being released on bail following 18 months in detention during the military-backed government's rule from 2006 to 2008.
He was convicted in absentia of charges including corruption, money laundering, and involvement in a 2004 grenade attack on a political rally for his political rival, Sheikh Hasina.
These convictions were overturned or stayed after Hasina's government's fall.
His return comes amid preparations for general elections scheduled for early 2026, under an interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus.
The elections follow a student-led uprising in 2024 that resulted in Hasina's removal and her subsequent flight to India.
The protests, initially sparked by opposition to a job quota system, escalated into broader anti-government demonstrations, leading to an estimated 1,400 deaths according to United Nations figures.
Hasina has since been sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the crackdown.
According to a December poll by the International Republican Institute, the BNP is the frontrunner for the election with 30 percent support.
The party has recently distanced itself from allies like Jamaat-e-Islami to adopt a more centrist approach.
However, challenges remain, including integrating party factions, maintaining law and order, and addressing potential unrest from Awami League supporters.
The Awami League was not allowed to participate in the elections.
Rahman's mother, Khaleda Zia, 80, is hospitalised in critical condition since November 2025.
She was the BNP's acting chairman since 2018 and was jailed most of the times during Hasina's administration.

items.title: United States capture Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro

s: The president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro, has been captured by the United States on Saturday at around 3 am UTC-4, according to a post by US president Donald Trump on social media.
Trump has told reporters Maduro had been “in a house that was more like a fortress”, in the country’s capital, Caracas.
Trump justified this action by claiming that Maduro is the leader of the Cartel de los Soles, and pushing illegal immigration of dangerous individuals in the United States.
Yván Gil Pinto, Venezuela’s foreign minister, said the country has requested a United Nations Security Council meeting to be held after the attack.
The BBC reports airstrikes in Caracas targeting La Carlota, an airbase and Fort Tiuna, a military base where the United States suspected Maduro to be located, and in other locations.
According to local authorities there has been civilian deaths and injuries, but the exact numbers are still unknown.
It was also reported by the BBC that the operation was orchestrated by a {CIA infiltration of the Venezuelan government.
France 24 reported that the CIA had been monitoring his “every movement since August”, despite Maduro’s efforts to change location regularly.
It was also reported that the operation involved more than 150 military aircraft, including one helicopter that was to capture Maduro.

According to the United States authorities, the Delta Force special operation force, arrived at Maduro’s location at “2:01 a.m. local time” and were able to capture him before he could get into his solid steel safe room (sources contradict however, on his exact location at that point.
Some sources reported that Trump said Maduro was almost in his safe room whilst others said he was sleeping in his bed).
They then relocated the “indicted persons” on a ship after crossing the coastline of Venezuela at 3:29 am.

Trump later revealed that Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, was also captured, and both were on board the USS Iwo Jima (LHD-7) with destination the southern district of New York, ultimately to be prosecuted.

Attorney General Pam Bondi was quoted by the BBC saying “[he will] face the full wrath of American justice on American soil in American courts” and, according to CNN, announced an indictment for leading “state‐sponsored gangs” and supporting drug trafficking.
Venezuelan authorities also reported other strikes, said to be made with the intent of seizing their oil and minerals, and have declared national emergency.
They, along with Cuba, Colombia, Iran and Russia, have denounced the action as a “serious military aggression”.
Argentine’s president, Javier Milei supported the action.
Venezuela’s vice‐president, Delcy Rodríguez called for Maduro and his wife to be released, saying the operation violated the country’s territorial integrity.
The BBC stated that these strikes follow a string of more than 30 strikes on Venezuelan vessels, and a strike on a “dock area” in Maracaibo, resulting in the death of more than 110 people.
The Trump administration stated that it is engaging in “non‐international armed conflict with […] alleged drug traffickers”.
According to the BBC, legal experts doubt the legality of these actions, saying the strikes are not against "lawful military targets".
According to CNN, Trump also justified not advising Congress before the operation to avoid a "leak", which drew criticisms from Democratic lawmakers.

After the capture, the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment against Maduro in which Maduro and others were charged with “conspiracy to commit narco‐terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine”.

According to the BBC, Maduro has denied this and has said before that Trump’s actual goal is to get access to Venezuela’s oil reserves, as indicated by the United States’ confiscation of several oil tankers.

items.title: Kyiv street to be named for former Ukrainian parliament chairman Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv

s: A street in Kyiv will be named after the former Speaker of the Parliament Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv.
The initiative to commemorate the prominent Ukrainian politician was supported by 57% of participants in a public poll on "Kyiv Digital" application.
On January 1, Maryna Poroshenko, the leader of “European Solidarity”, announced the street name in the Kyiv City Council and on Facebook.
As the result, a section along Mariinsky Park – from Hrushevskoho Street to Parkova Road – will bear the politician's name, named "Andrei Parubia Street".
In December, former President of Ukraine and head of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko asked the residents of Kyiv to support the vote to name the street after Parubiy.
The street had no name at the time of the proposal.
"This place is significant for our team and for Andriy himself — a significant part of his journey is connected with it," Poroshenko said.
On October 1, 2025, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree awarding Parubiy the title of Hero of Ukraine.

A petition to award the title of Hero of Ukraine to Parubiy was registered on the presidential website on September 2, gaining 25,000 signatures, which was necessary for the proposal to be considered by President.
The Verkhovna Rada, the Ukrainian parliament, also supported the request.
Parubiy was among several people who were conferred Heroes of Ukraine.
Others were writer Volodymyr Vakulenko and student and footballer Stepan Chubenko.
Poroshenko lauded the decision, recalling that "Parubiy dedicated his entire life to serving Ukraine".
Andriy Parubiy, 54, who served as the Chairman of Verkhovna Rada from 14 April 2016 to 29 August 2019, was shot and killed in Lviv on 30 August 2025.
He died at the scene from injuries.
The killing happened amid the Russian invasion, which started in 2022.
The shooter managed to escape.
Later, Ukrainian authorities detained a suspect, and allege there is a Russian link to the killing.
Parubiy was an active participant of Euromaidan.
He also served as Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine from February till August 2014.
The suspected killer of Ukrainian lawmaker Andriy Parubiy admitted on 2 September his role in the killing.
He claimed to have comitted the crime in an act of "revenge" against the country’s authorities.
He denied having worked with Russian special services.

items.title: "I came to be the manager ... not the coach": Manchester United fire head coach Ruben Amorim

s: On Monday, Manchester United football team fired its coach Ruben Amorim after fourteen months in the role.
Amorim had met with Omar Berrada, chief executive officer of the team, and Jason Wilcox, the team's director of football, on Friday morning.
While discussing his preferred 3-4-3 style, the conversation reportedly quickly spiraled out of control, resulting in Amorim losing his job.
Manchester United announced the news of the dismissal at around 10 a.m. on Monday.
After the team drawing against Leeds F.C.
1-1, the coach had said at a press conference that he came to be "the manager, not the coach" and said Wilcox should "do his job".
Wilcox intended the meeting to focus on the recent draw.

Manchester United was sixth in the Premier League, almost not classifying for the Champions League, less than four points ahead of Sunderland A.F.C., Everton F.C., Fulham F.C., Brighton & Hove Albion F.C., Newcastle United and Brentford F.C., a precarious position, El Pais reported.
Former Manchester United captain Gary Neville communicated to Sky Sports News that he expected better performance, saying he "thought they'd get through another couple of weeks."

items.title: Homeland Security says Minneapolis woman shot by ICE officer dies

s: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported Wednesday that a woman shot by a U.S.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis has died.
Homeland Security officials have described the shooting as an act of self-defense, while Minnesota governor Tim Walz and Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey have pushed back on this account.

DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin stated that the shooting occurred when ICE officers fired "defensive shots" in response to the woman "attempting to run over our law enforcement officers" with her vehicle.
Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem said the woman’s conduct was "an act of domestic terrorism."
The incident was under active investigation, with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) and the FBI taking over the case.
Walz said the state was working to learn more and asked residents to remain calm, while protest activity continued at the scene and a substantial law-enforcement presence remained in the area.
According to ABC News, Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, said in a statement that he was aware of the shooting and urged the agency to depart the city at once.
On social media, he stated the involvement of federal immigration officers was "causing chaos in our city.
He added that the city is "demanding ICE to leave the city immediately," and said officials "stand rock solid with our immigrant and refugee communities.
In a news conference, he disputed the account that the woman's vehicle was weaponized against the agent.

items.title: Roblox player uncovers cheating, awarded Guinness World Record

s: In early January, international media reported that Quinten Delaere, an 18-year-old, had been officially recognized by Guinness World Records after exposing cheating on the Roblox platform.
Delaere, known online as 'kannotlogin', used data analysis to demonstrate that the top times on the global leaderboard were achieved using illegal scripts.
Delaere was competing in a speed-running event for the game Ultimate Easy Obby.
The event was an official collaboration between Roblox and Guinness World Records.
Players had to complete a digital obstacle course as fast as possible.
According to JV, after weeks of practice, Delaere posted a time of 5 minutes and 48.96 seconds.
Before the competition closed, three unknown accounts posted times around 5 minutes and 42 seconds.
JV reported that Delaere, posting on Reddit, believed the times were humanly impossible.
Delaere conducted a digital forensic analysis and compiled a report alleging that the new records were fraudulent.
The report cited three technical points.
First, the analysis pointed to the timestamps of the badges earned by the rival accounts.
The data showed that badges were unlocked in a non-chronological order.
